Maria R.: Heads-up — customer 'AcmeHealth' is seeing intermittent outbound failures to our edge when they route through a transparent proxy + NAT gateway. Root log snippet: "upstream tls handshake failed: EOF". Any quick hypotheses?
Sam T.: is this only for TLS flows or plain http too?
Maria R.: Mostly TLS (443). Plain HTTP (80) looks fine. They say their proxy does TLS interception (corporate mitm) and also preserves source ports sometimes, but SNAT pool is small.
Devin L.: small SNAT pool + high concurrency = port exhaustion or very short-lived ports. If ports are reused you can get weird TCP resets and TLS errors.
Sam T.: also check hairpin/NAT reflection. If the proxy lives inside their network and NATs back to their gateway to reach our public IP, some boxes will fail TCP MUX.
Maria R.: They reported that when they increase ephemeral ports the failures drop. But they can't expand forever. They asked if we can provide a hostname to allowlist instead of IPs because their firewall is hostname-aware.
Devin L.: short answer: customers need IP ranges for allowlists. Hostname allowlisting is brittle because of CF/ELB fronting and IP churn. But we can offer a couple mitigations:
- recommend they allow our egress LB CIDR blocks (we have a published list)
- support a proxy-transparent healthcheck mode so their proxy won't break healthchecks
- if they must use hostname allowlists, they need to resolve DNS frequently and accept TTL changes.
Sam T.: also confirm proxy behavior for CONNECT vs passthrough. If the proxy rewrites SNI or does TLS-inspect, our SNI-based routing may pick a different backend and break client cert expectations.
Maria R.: good point. Customer says TLS-inspect rewrites cert chain. Our ALB sees client hello and then 502s.
Devin L.: action items I suggest:
1) Ask customer to add our published LB ranges and the healthcheck source IPs to their outbound allowlist. Link: https://internal.redwood/egress-ip-list (public doc TBD).
2) If they use transparent proxy, request they enable NAT port preservation or enlarge ephemeral port range to avoid port exhaustion. Example sysctl on linux: `net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range`
3) For TLS-inspect cases, ask them to whitelist our hostnames on their proxy (so CONNECT flows are passed through) or install our CA on their proxy to avoid SNI rewrite.
4) Short-term workaround: lower concurrency from client side (max_conns=8) or introduce client-side keepalives to reduce ephemeral port churn.
Maria R.: I'll draft a short checklist for them. Can infra-provide a one-off static egress IP for this customer (Dedicated static NAT) so the customer can allow one IP instead of a broad range?
Devin L.: we have Dedicated static-egress product but there's a lead time. For Hosted customers we can sometimes provide a pinned egress NAT from a /29 for an SSOee request. Need SRE approval.
Sam T.: I'll spin up a quick healthcheck that probes via a proxy (using curl --proxy) to reproduce. Adding the command here:
```
curl -v --proxy http://proxy.corp:3128 --connect-timeout 10 https://edge.redwood.example/status
```
Use --local-port to simulate port exhaustion: `--local-port 40000-40100`.
infra-bot: NOTE: logged ticket #INC-2026 for "Outbound proxy + NAT hairpinning causing TLS EOFs" (assigned to eng-infra).
Maria R.: thanks all. I'll send the checklist and include the suggested curl tests. If SRE can confirm we can offer a short-lived static egress for them, that might unblock their firewall change. :thumbsup:
Sam T.: ping me if you want me to run the curl probe against their proxy endpoint, happy to help.
Devin L.: also adding: ask them to capture tcpdump of a failing flow (client, proxy, gateway) so we can look at SYN/FIN reuse patterns.
Maria R.: noted — I'll collect and post back.
